facts.raw_span: 6-month history of progressive dysarthria and dysphagia
Family history notable for a relative with memory problems after age 80
Cognitive impairment
Vertical gaze palsy
Tongue atrophy
Pyramidal signs
Severe loss of dopamine transporter binding in basal ganglia
Almost total loss in caudate nucleus
Left caudate: 0.35 (normal 1.55-2.07)
Heterozygous pathogenic variant of TBK1 gene (p.E643del) identified by whole-exon sequencing
Autoimmune encephalitis antibodies negative in serum and CSF
Large-amplitude, long-duration motor unit potential in frontalis, mentalis, orbicularis oculi, and genioglossus muscles

concepts.preferred_label: Frontotemporal dementia and parkinsonism linked to chromosome 12
concepts.why: The combination of progressive dysarthria, dysphagia, cognitive impairment, vertical gaze palsy, tongue atrophy, pyramidal signs, and severe loss of dopamine transporter binding in basal ganglia, along with a heterozygous pathogenic variant of the TBK1 gene, supports this diagnosis.
The presence of vertical gaze palsy, cognitive impairment, and severe loss of dopamine transporter binding in basal ganglia are characteristic of this disease.

The combination of progressive dysarthria, dysphagia, cognitive impairment, tongue atrophy, and pyramidal signs, along with a heterozygous pathogenic variant of the TBK1 gene, supports this diagnosis.

concepts.why: The presence of progressive dysarthria, dysphagia, cognitive impairment, tongue atrophy, and large-amplitude, long-duration motor unit potentials, along with a heterozygous pathogenic variant of the TBK1 gene, supports this diagnosis.

rationales.F01: Progressive dysarthria and dysphagia are common in frontotemporal dementia and parkinsonism linked to chromosome 12 and amyotrophic lateral sclerosis with frontotemporal dementia
rationales.F04: Vertical gaze palsy is a characteristic feature of progressive supranuclear palsy

frontier_selector.runner_up: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis with frontotemporal dementia
frontier_selector.rationale: Vertical gaze palsy and severe loss of dopamine transporter binding in basal ganglia are key findings that align with Progressive supranuclear palsy, while the presence of tongue atrophy and large-amplitude motor unit potentials also support Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis with frontotemporal dementia as a close runner-up.
